#3070. Netflix Engagement Growth Is Slowing. Here’s Why I Bought More Anyway.

Netflix's core competitive advantage should drive great long-term results.

Netflix (NFLX -0.86%) is seeing a decline in the number of hours its members watch. The company's What We Watched report showed a 2% year-over-year increase in total viewing hours in the first half of the year.

Despite the deterioration in this key metric, I bought more Netflix shares a couple of weeks ago. With the stock trading close to the same level as the end of October, I think it's still a great opportunity for investors. Here's why I bought more.

Netflix doesn't just compete with other premium streaming services; it competes with social media, podcasts, video games, YouTube, and tons of free entertainment. This is a dynamic that management has pointed out for years as an indication that it has a lot of room to grow.

Now, it appears that free entertainment has taken a bite out of its engagement. That's not necessarily a bad thing for the core subscription offering. Netflix is positioned as a premium product relative to free offerings like Alphabet's YouTube. It offers premium content like big-budget drama series and live events.

For a growing number of users, Netflix is becoming appointment viewing rather than something you put on after a long day at work when you don't have a plan to watch anything in particular.

Granted, it still serves as background entertainment for many people. There will always be room in Netflix's content budget for low-cost, high-volume productions. For example, it struck a deal with The Ringer to bring video podcasts to its platform.

Netflix's scale relative to other media companies is a huge advantage. It can spend more on content than anyone else because it can amortize that cost across a larger viewership. Netflix also has more data on how much its viewers actually value a particular piece of content, or how likely they are to value a new series or film. As a result, it can be extremely effective with its content budget.

The result is steadily expanding operating margin, growing earnings, and strong free cash flow. Management returns that excess free cash flow to shareholders through share repurchases, helping produce strong earnings-per-share growth.

The continued operating leverage in the business remains very appealing, and there appears to be room to keep expanding operating margin over the coming years. That means even modest revenue growth, combined with the share repurchase plans, can result in very strong earnings-per-share growth.

But with investors worried about the company's user engagement, the stock price dropped to just 17.7 times forward earnings expectations. At that price, Netflix can see a further slowdown in revenue growth and still produce solid returns for investors.

Management doesn't expect revenue growth to slow much more than it has. CFO Spencer Neumann reiterated expectations for double-digit revenue growth, expanding profit margin, and growing free cash flow during the company's third-quarter earnings call. Achieving all of those makes the stock an excellent buy at the current price.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There’s not long to wait until Percy Jackson returns for another mythological adventure, with season 3 of “Percy Jackson and the Olympians” arriving on Disney+ on November 20. Based on Rick Riordan’s third novel, the new instalment sees Walker Scobell’s Percy embark on a dangerous quest after Annabeth Chase (Leah Sava Jeffries) is captured by the forces of Kronos.

With Grover (Aryan Simhadri) by his side, Percy must rescue his friend, free a goddess in chains and confront a prophecy that could spell disaster for Olympus. There are plenty of familiar faces returning, alongside exciting newcomers including Nico and Bianca di Angelo, while Thalia Grace (Tamara Smart) looks set to play an increasingly important role. But before we dive back into Camp Half-Blood, here are five things worth remembering from the first two seasons.

Fair warning: I’ll be spoiling major events from seasons 1 and 2. So, without further ado, here are five things you should remember before “Percy Jackson” season 3.

Thalia Grace’s return at the end of season 2 comes with a major twist that changes everything heading into season 3. In the original books, Zeus turned his daughter into a pine tree to save her life after monsters mortally wounded her. However, the series reveals that he actually imprisoned her as punishment after she refused to obey him and become his weapon in the coming war.

When Clarisse (Dior Goodjohn) uses the Golden Fleece to heal Camp Half-Blood’s protective borders, Thalia returns to human form. The revelation also raises questions about who the demigods can trust. Chiron (Glynn Turman) and the camp’s leaders had hidden the truth about Thalia from Percy, Annabeth and Grover for years. Her hatred of Zeus could also bring her closer to Luke Castellan (Charlie Bushnell) and Kronos, although where her loyalties ultimately lie remains unclear.

Most importantly, Thalia’s return complicates the Great Prophecy. As Zeus’s daughter, she’s another child of the Big Three who could fulfil the prediction, meaning Percy might not be the only demigod capable of deciding Olympus’s fate.

Thalia’s return wasn’t just a side effect of healing Camp Half-Blood. It also gave Kronos another way to threaten Olympus. The Great Prophecy states that a child of one of the “Big Three” gods (Zeus, Poseidon or Hades) who reaches the age of 16 will decide whether Olympus survives or falls.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Before Thalia returned, Percy was the main demigod connected to the prophecy. Now, Zeus’s daughter could also fulfil it, making the situation much more complicated. The two immediately clash after Thalia wakes up, setting up a potential rivalry between them.

Her return also gives Kronos another opportunity to turn a powerful demigod against the gods. Thalia has plenty of reasons to hate Zeus, which could make her vulnerable to his influence. As season 3 approaches, both Percy and Thalia could play a major role in deciding the fate of Olympus.

After the battle at Thalia’s tree, Percy briefly sees his father, Poseidon (Toby Stephens), in a vision while unconscious. Poseidon tells him that the war against Kronos has officially begun and asks Percy’s Cyclops half-brother, Tyson (Daniel Diemer), to help make weapons in the underwater forges.

Tyson happily accepts, finally feeling like he has a place alongside his father. However, his departure leaves Percy facing the growing threat on his own. While Tyson gets a chance to help the gods prepare for war, Percy must return to Camp Half-Blood and deal with the dangers ahead.

The moment also shows that the conflict with Kronos is much bigger than the fight at camp. With Tyson helping build weapons beneath the sea, season 3 could explore more of the underwater world and Poseidon’s role in the coming war.

Luke Castellan has become an increasingly dangerous threat by the end of season 2. Although Clarisse successfully retrieves the Golden Fleece for Camp Half-Blood, Luke’s forces still achieve something important: Thalia is brought back to life, giving Kronos another powerful demigod who could join his side.

The attack also exposes how poorly Camp Half-Blood is being run. After King Tantalus (Timothy Simons) is killed during the siege, Dionysus (Jason Mantzoukas) reluctantly takes charge again but does little to organize the campers. Instead, Percy steps up and gives an inspiring speech, encouraging everyone to defend their home.

This also helps explain why Luke has turned against the Olympian gods. He believes they mistreat their children and care more about their own power than the demigods’ lives. With Zeus’s treatment of Thalia only adding to that argument, Luke has plenty of ammunition to convince others to join Kronos. Heading into season 3, he’s still a major threat to Percy and everyone at Camp Half-Blood.

Season 3 adapts “The Titan’s Curse,” which sees Annabeth Chase captured by Kronos’ forces. Her disappearance sets Percy on another dangerous quest to rescue his friend, but it also puts his biggest weakness to the test: his loyalty to the people he loves.

Percy has always been willing to put himself in danger to protect his friends, even when it means ignoring warnings or going against the gods. With Annabeth’s life at stake, that side of him is likely to become even more important in season 3.

The trailer also shows Percy carrying the weight of the sky, a burden traditionally associated with the Titan Atlas. It’s another example of how far he’s willing to go to protect the people closest to him. As the Great Prophecy draws closer, Percy will have to balance his feelings for Annabeth and his friends with the fate of Olympus.

"Percy Jackson and the Olympians" season 3 premieres with two episodes on Disney Plus on November 20. After that, new episodes arrive weekly on Fridays.

#3067. Apple Maps in iOS 27 has hidden new feature I’ve been loving

iOS 27 gave Apple Maps a handful of new features, and my favorite is one that keeps offering fresh updates every week: Local Lists.

Apple Maps has long offered a ‘Guides’ feature where you can browse curated collections of places worth checking out. Sometimes they’re created by Apple’s editorial team, other times by celebrities or in conjunction with current events.

But in iOS 27, there’s a new feature—Local Lists—that’s sort of an extension of Guides, but it gets updated weekly with the latest trending places.

Here’s how Apple describes it, via Apple Newsroom:

I’ve always enjoyed browsing Guides in Maps to help find new places. But Local Lists are a great expansion of the idea, especially since they’re updated all the time. I’m always up for trying a new trending restaurant, and now Maps makes it easy to stay on top of what’s new.

Even if you’ve been using iOS 27 for months, there’s a good chance you’ve never seen Local Lists. That’s because they’re pretty hidden.

To find the feature, tap into the search field in Maps and scroll down to see a new ‘Trending Restaurants’ section. On my iPhone 18 Pro, by default this section gets hidden behind the keyboard, so you have to first scroll and dismiss the keyboard to see it.

Trending Restaurants are ranked from 1-20. The search screen shows only a handful, but you can tap to view the full list. For example, if you open the ‘Trending Restaurants in New York’ list, you’ll see 20 places worth checking out.

How does a restaurant make the list? Per the in-app explanation, the list contains “Restaurants climbing in popularity this week, based on what people view, share, and interact with on Apple Maps.”

Since these Trending Restaurants lists update weekly, Apple says you’ll want to save any places you plan to visit. There’s a convenient + button next to each listing.

It’s unclear exactly how many different parts of the US have localized lists in iOS 27. But if you poke around and find the full collection of Local Lists, there are 1,021 total—so you’ll probably have one in your area.

You can browse all available lists by opening a Trending Restaurants list then tapping where you see the Apple logo and ‘Local Lists’ near the text that says when it was last updated.

Have you used Local Lists in iOS 27’s Maps app yet? Let us know what you think via the comments.

#3066. AT&T vs. Verizon: Which Telecom Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

AT&T and Verizon both trade at similar valuations, but their paths diverge sharply in other areas.

AT&T focuses on a simplified business model emphasizing fiber and 5G deployment, while Verizon leverages its massive scale and global connectivity services. Both companies are navigating a capital-intensive industry where reliable network performance and consistent cash flow are the primary drivers of investor returns.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached $128.9 billion, representing growth of 3.5% compared to the prior year. Net income for this period was $13.1 billion, resulting in a net margin of 10.1%. This growth reflects steady progress in adding new wireless and fiber customers even as the company navigates a competitive pricing environment.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 1.6x, showing how much debt the conglomerate uses relative to its equity. The current ratio, which measures the ability to cover short-term debts with current assets, was 0.9x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow reached $19.4 billion, which is cash left after paying for operating costs and equipment.

Verizon operates one of the largest wireless networks in the world, supporting approximately 147 million total retail connections. Its customer base includes nearly all of the Fortune 500 companies, highlighting its role in critical business infrastructure. Verizon recently strengthened its fiber capabilities through the acquisition of Frontier Communications and a multi-billion dollar artificial intelligence partnership with Amazon (AMZN -0.29%).

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached $139.4 billion, which is an increase of 1.4% over the previous twelve-month period. Net income for the company reached $16.4 billion, reflecting a net margin of 11.8%. Slower revenue growth compared to its peer reflects a highly mature wireless market where capturing new market share requires significant investment.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio was 0.9x, suggesting that short-term assets are slightly lower than short-term liabilities. The debt-to-equity ratio was 1.7x, reflecting the substantial capital needed to maintain and upgrade its national network. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was $19.7 billion.

Verizon must navigate pricing pressure from rivals and satellite providers like EchoStar (ECHO +1.91%). The company is also integrating large acquisitions like Frontier Communications, which can lead to unexpected expenses or logistical hurdles. Similar to its peers, it faces regulatory scrutiny over legacy network materials and the ongoing threat of sophisticated cyberattacks on critical infrastructure.

Both stocks trade at identical Forward P/E multiples based on future earnings estimates. AT&T offers a lower P/S ratio, comparing its price to sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

AT&T and Verizon are mature telecom companies, and as such, their share price appreciation is unlikely to deliver outsized returns. Instead, it's their dividend payments that are a key factor to investor returns. That's why the better stock for 2027 is Verizon.

Both offer robust forward dividend yields. AT&T sports a 5% yield as of the week ending Nov. 13, while Verizon is higher at 6%. However, Verizon has raised its dividend payment for the last 20 consecutive years.

AT&T stopped growing its dividend after it divested entertainment companies acquired under previous management in an ill-fated attempt to attract consumers to its services. In fact, the telecom giant cut its dividend nearly in half in 2022 as part of this divestiture, and payouts have remained at that level ever since.

The two companies are fairly similar across share price valuations, debt-to-equity ratios, and free cash flow generation, which is used to pay down debt and fund dividends. So of the two, with Verizon's impressive streak of dividend increases, it is the better stock for investors to buy.

#3065. How Microcredentials Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI

IEEE Credentialing Program offers ethics and compliance training

Kaitlyn Ridel is the IEEE microcredentials marketing specialist.

Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics, governance, and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges.

“AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance.

Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the International Organization for Standardization.

The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias, security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap.

Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies.

Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust.

Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance.

Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program.

Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment.

For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles.

Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards, most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle.

The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust.

To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert.

Kaitlyn Ridel is a marketing specialist for the IEEE Microcredentialing Program

#3064. This tiny iOS 27 camera feature really makes a huge difference

When shooting both photos and videos on my iPhone, I make regular use of a few different third-party apps, mostly because I like to take manual control.

But a combination of the new Pro controls on the iPhone 18 Pro and a new feature introduced with iOS 27 means there are more times when I can stick to Apple’s stock Camera app. If you aren’t already using customizable controls, I highly recommend doing so …

Developers know that a big reason for using third-party camera apps is being able to use them in much the same way you would a standalone camera. A key part of this is having easy access to manual control over things like aperture (on the iPhone 18 Pro), shutter speed, white balance, and choosing between manual and auto focus. Those settings are right there on the main screen of almost all third-party apps.

With the iPhone 18 Pro, the same set of controls are also available in Apple’s stock camera app. By default, these are tucked inside a menu, requiring an initial tap to open it. As we noted back in September, however, iOS 27 brings customizable controls to the camera app.

Simply open the menu and tap the Edit button (top-left when holding the phone vertically) and you can add any of the controls to the main screen. This makes them available in a single tap.

Aperture, shutter speed, and white balance as these are the three main manual controls I use. Exposure compensation, because sometimes the only reason I want to take manual control is to increase or decrease the exposure, and that provides a faster way of doing so (quicker than the alternative drag up/down within the photo, in my experience). Finally, I have one-tap access to the histogram to help in setting exposure.

It’s a similar story in video mode. I again have aperture and white balance along with exposure compensation and the histogram. But here I add instant access to frame-rate and focus modes (as I’m more likely to switch focus mode when shooting video).

Of course, third-party apps still have an important role, but this one change has made a big difference to me when using the stock camera app for both photos and video.

Do you make use of this feature yourself? If so, please share the details in the comments.

Denzel and Davis both throw heat in 'Fences'

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Verdict: This period drama is a well-executed adaptation of August Wilson's award-winning 1985 play of the same name. Unfortunately, it notably feels like you're watching a play; it struggles to make the case for why it's a dramatic work of cinema as opposed to a theatrical revival. But as Denzel Washington and Viola Davis start pitching a perfect game, you stop nitpicking and let the performances take over.

Where to watch: Stream "Fences" for free on Tubi or YouTube

"Fences" was a movie I circled on my calendar as I made my way through this year-long Denzel Watchathon. This is considered a seminal work in the legendary actor's career. It's his third directorial effort in his filmography and by far the best. It also earned him his seventh Oscar nomination as an actor (his second of three he'd earn in the 2010s alone).

Once you watch it, it's no surprise why this performance makes the highlight reel. This movie is essentially crafted to serve his character, except for the few scenes where it's designed to highlight Viola Davis. She plays Denzel's on-screen wife in this period drama film, and I'd argue it's her performance that's the more impressive of the two.

Unfortunately, if I have to nitpick, this strength is also the movie's biggest weakness. "Fences" is adapted from August Wilson's 1985 play of the same name. That play was a roaring success, earning Wilson both a Pulitzer and a Tony Award in 1987. Watching this film adaptation, one wouldn't be shocked if Denzel and Wilson (who also wrote the screenplay for this movie) didn't change a thing from the Broadway version. The entire time, it feels unmistakably like you're watching a play.

This isn't inherently a bad thing; I often like movies adapted from plays, and to be clear, I thought this film was excellent. But unlike, say, "A Few Good Men," I failed to see what was added to the performances, to the story, etc., by turning Wilson's play into a cinematic experience. If you had simply had this same cast act out the play on a stage and filmed it on a Sony Handycam, it'd probably be just as good.

If you want to watch this movie before you read on, I have good news! It's currently streaming for free on Tubi, one of the best free streaming services we've tested. You can also stream it for free on YouTube (with ads).

Malcolm has been with the Streaming team at Tom's Guide since 2023, reviewing dozens of movies each year so you don't have to watch the bad ones.

Here are some of the other Denzel Washington movies I've covered to date in my Denzel Watchathon:

Read more: Every Denzel Watchathon movie so far

The sixth installment in August Wilson's 10-part "Pittsburgh Cycle," "Fences," centers around Troy. Portrayed by Denzel Washington in this adaptation, he's a middle-aged man working as a sanitation worker. He appears to be an ordinary working-class Pittsburgher, albeit sans Yinzer accent. But as the story unfolds, it's quickly apparent that Troy wasn't always destined for an ordinary life.

Troy, as revealed by his longtime friend, Bono (Stephen McKinley Henderson), was at one point one of the best baseball players in America. But he had the bad luck of being a Black player in the years before Jackie Robinson broke the color barrier in Major League Baseball. So while his Negro League career earned him plaudits and adulation, it didn't exactly bring in the cash. And you can only dine on praise for so long before reality sets in.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Complicating things is ... well, everything else. His marriage to Rose (Viola Davis) appears healthy, but early on in the movie there are hints this isn't the case. It's clear that money can be a pain point for Troy, who now has less of it than ever because he's no longer collecting part of his brother's (Mykelti Williamson) disability check from the Army. When Troy's 34-year-old son, Lyons (Russell Hornsby), comes asking for money, it's clear that Troy thinks he'll never see that money again, and that he doesn't have enough cash to waste. Even on family.

But it's not Lyons's relationship with his father at the core of "Fences." Instead, the film focuses on Troy's relationship with his other son, Cory. He's 17 years old and the only child produced by Troy and Rose's marriage. His relationship with his dad is somewhat rocky and complicated by the fact that colleges are recruiting Cory for football. Troy, a former pro athlete who now makes a living hauling trash, wants Cory to avoid sports entirely for fear that it will lead him down the same path Troy went down.

Davis is more subtle in her performance. She's not given a ton to do at first, but then she's given some devastating news in a later scene, and it allows her to steal the scene. From that moment on, she steals the entire movie.

Despite all this focus on Troy and his sons, it's Viola Davis who steals the movie as Rose. Denzel is supposed to be excellent in this movie. He's given incredible lines. He's the main character. Every character exists in this story to be a reflection of his impact on their lives or to highlight a trial and tribulation Troy has had to deal with. There's a scene early on where Cory asks why Troy doesn't like him, and Denzel just cooks, as the Gen Z youths would say. In fact, if you've seen a scene from this movie on TikTok, it's probably this scene of Denzel as Troy taking his son down a peg.

Davis is more subtle in her performance. She's not given a ton to do at first, but then she's given some devastating news in a later scene, and it allows her to steal the scene. From that moment on, she steals the entire movie.

In that aforementioned scene, she's not openly weeping, sobbing, or screaming at the top of her lungs, all of which would be perfectly reasonable responses given the news she just received. However, she manages to do a feat of physical acting where snot just runs from her nostrils. It's the clear aftermath of a moment of grief, underlying the fact that she's not nearly as composed as she's forcing herself to appear on the outside.

When I say that Davis steals this movie and doesn't let go, I mean it. She was the lone Oscar winner for "Fences," deservedly taking home the Oscar for Best Supporting Actress. It might be the first movie since "The Manchurian Candidate" where I felt that an actress took the spotlight from Denzel and there was simply nothing he could do about it.

But again, Denzel is great in this movie. He earns an Oscar nomination; the movie itself earns a Best Picture nomination, in no small part due to his performance and direction. It's a tough watch at times. Because it feels like a play but lacks the intimate, almost physical connection between thespian and theatergoer, it can also lose your interest on occasion.

That all is quickly brushed aside, though, as the film reaches its climax. The performances at the center of this movie are the definition of must-watch. And now that it's currently available to stream at home for free, you really have no excuse not to check it out if you haven't already.

#3061. iOS 27.3 adds three new features I’ve used almost every day

iOS 27.3 is coming next month, and during the beta so far there are three new features I’ve been using almost every day.

Siri AI in iOS 27 brings major upgrades by providing world knowledge, personal context features, and being more conversational than ever. But one previously announced Siri improvement—an expanded set of actions for Apple apps—didn’t make the cut in iOS 27.0.

Now in iOS 27.3, though, Apple is rolling out its first set of new app actions for Siri AI.

Siri AI has new capabilities across apps like Calendar, Files, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. It’s a big step toward making voice-driven computing more powerful on Apple platforms, and I’ve had fun experimenting with everything new Siri can do.

Read more: iOS 27.3 expands Siri AI with many new capabilities across Apple apps

Apple Health gets a big overhaul in iOS 27.3, with a fresh design and new features that utilize Apple Intelligence for more personalized health insights. Per Apple:

The updated experience includes a new Insights tab that surfaces timely, holistic summaries spanning heart, sleep, readiness, fitness, vitals, and cycle tracking data throughout the day. A dedicated For You section delivers intelligent recommendations tailored to a user’s daily habits — such as practical guidance to adjust a wind-down routine following consecutive nights of interrupted sleep. The app pairs data with dynamic health content, offering educational videos and articles featuring Health app clinical experts.

In my testing so far, I’ve especially enjoyed getting up-to-date guidance every day on my health metrics, browsing the deep collection of new educational videos and articles, and understanding all the factors that contribute to longevity. I think Apple is moving the right direction with this update.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds all-new Apple Health app, details here

If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4, iOS 27.3 adds a powerful new feature called Siri Recap that “ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory.”

Siri Recap functions like an outsourced short-term memory reserve. The data it collects is saved inside the Siri app in a new Recaps tab, where it lives for seven days and is then deleted—unless you manually save a specific recap.

So far in the beta, I’ve found the summaries Siri generates to strike a good balance of being helpful but not too invasive. It reminds me of key details, but there’s nothing I’ve seen that feels overly sensitive or personalized. That may change over time the more I use it, but so far I think this could prove a really valuable feature.

Read more: watchOS 27.3 adds new Apple Watch feature that I absolutely love

#3060. NXP: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Factory utilization in the mid-80% range and a path to 60% gross margins suggest NXP is positioned to convert structural growth into shareholder returns.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 27, 2026, NXP (NXPI -0.82%) announced a 19% year-over-year increase in quarterly revenue to $3.79 billion. Demand for chips that power software-defined vehicles and physical artificial intelligence creates structural growth drivers across core end markets.

Automobile manufacturers are shifting toward centralized computing architectures that require up to three times more semiconductor content per vehicle. NXP is positioning its software-defined vehicle (SDV) portfolio, which refers to computing platforms where software controls car functions, to capture this expanding value.

Data centers represent a growing market for control-plane microcontrollers, which are dedicated microprocessors that coordinate system hardware and manage data traffic. Management expanded its outlook as server architectures adopt higher-performance processing units.

Free cash flow, which measures cash left over after operating costs and capital investments, reached $1.21 billion in the third quarter. Management is redirecting cash toward share buybacks as capital needs for manufacturing joint ventures normalize.

Factory utilization rates are running in the mid-80% range, and leadership expects higher production volume to drive operational efficiencies across manufacturing sites.

NXP relies on long-term architecture transitions in automotive and industrial markets to secure multiyear customer contracts.

#3059. Perplexity brings AI agents feature called Teammates to the Mac

This week, Perplexity has deployed its new proactive agentic AI feature called Teammates to the Mac. Perplexity Teammates were previously limited to iOS and the web.

Similar to Grok Bot, Perplexity Teammates are task-oriented proactive agentic AI threads that work for you without constantly being prompted. Meta Muse and ChatGPT Dots are similar, but use a single chat model rather than supporting multiple instances.

Teammates are a team of AI agents that own ongoing work. Give a teammate a responsibility, such as managing a growth campaign, triaging incoming bug reports, tracking your metrics, or researching a new market, and it owns that work around the clock. It plans the tasks, brings in more agents when the work grows, and follows through until the result is ready for your review.

Access to Teammates currently requires a paid Perplexity Max subscription. The feature builds on top of Perplexity’s existing AI orchestration system.

#3056. Epic formally asks SCOTUS to uphold contempt ruling against Apple

Epic Games has submitted its official response to Apple’s Supreme Court appeal, urging the justices to uphold the contempt ruling over App Store payment restrictions. Here are the details.

As most 9to5Mac readers probably know, Apple and Epic Games have been engaged in a lengthy legal battle since 2020, when Epic sued Apple after Fortnite was removed from the App Store.

The move came after Epic remotely activated an alternative payment system that bypassed Apple’s In-App Purchase system.

Although the court largely sided with Apple, it did rule that the company could no longer prevent developers from directing users to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.

Apple ultimately allowed those links, but imposed new restrictions, including a 27% commission on external purchases, in addition to new rules limiting how developers could display buttons and links to alternative payment methods.

Epic challenged those restrictions, and the court agreed that Apple had violated the original injunction, holding the company in civil contempt.

Apple has since attempted multiple times to overturn that ruling, arguing that the original injunction contained no explicit prohibition on imposing those restrictions.

Epic, on the other hand, argues that Apple deliberately circumvented the court order by introducing new rules designed to achieve the same result as those originally prohibited.

In May, Apple appealed to the Supreme Court, which agreed in June to hear the case. Apple submitted its opening brief in September, followed by supporting briefs from the U.S. government and several legal and business groups.

Those included the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, Chamber of Progress, and several former federal antitrust enforcers. In a nutshell, the U.S. government argued that the original injunction did not clearly prohibit Apple’s 27% commission on external purchases, but maintained that the company was correctly held in contempt for restricting how developers could display external payment buttons.

In its opening brief, Apple argues, citing multiple legal precedents, that courts must enforce the letter of an injunction rather than its broader spirit.

According to the company, there was nothing in the original injunction explicitly prohibiting it from charging commissions on external purchases or imposing additional restrictions on payment links, so it should not be held in contempt for conduct that the court order did not clearly prohibit.

In its response filed today, Epic disputes Apple’s interpretation of the injunction, arguing that the company “attempts to avoid contempt by proposing an extreme legal standard.”

[Apple] argues that a court can find contempt only if an injunction spells out the exact practice at issue–so an injunction barring Apple’s then-existing anti-steering rules left it free to implement new ones that prevent steering just as effectively. Nothing in this Court’s precedents supports that approach, which would reduce injunctions to a never-ending game of whack-a-mole.

Epic argues that “Apple devised a plan to circumvent the injunction,” claiming that “Apple chose a rate of 27% for the commission, knowing that, when combined with the developers’ payment-handling costs (more than 3%), the rate for linked-out purchases would be higher than the rate for purchases using Apple’s payment system.”

As an Apple executive admitted, every “linked-out transaction is going to be more expensive to any developer * * * than an IAP transaction at 30 percent.” Apple simultaneously commissioned a “sham” report to try to provide an economic justification for the commission; the report contained an “entirely manufactured” rationale for the 27% rate.

The company also argues that “Apple tried to cover up its scheme to circumvent the injunction” by asserting privilege over more than 57,000 documents, and points to Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers’ finding that “its Vice President of Finance ‘outright lied under oath’ when he testified about when Apple decided to impose the new commission.”

Finally, Epic asks the Supreme Court to uphold the contempt ruling against Apple or, if the justices decide to clarify the legal standard for contempt, to send the case back to the lower courts for reconsideration under that standard.

With Epic’s response now filed, Apple has until December 14 to submit its final brief before oral arguments take place on January 11, 2027.

The Innocn E49M1R delivers massive, dual-27-inch screen real estate in a unique flat form factor, backed by punchy Mini-LED backlighting and plenty of ports. The lack of USB-C Power Delivery and edge wash-out from sitting too close hold it back slightly — though if you have a deep desk and run a desktop PC, there’s no monitor quite like it.

Widest, flat super ultrawide monitor available

Deep blacks thanks to Mini-LED backlighting

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The Innocn E49M1R isn’t your standard super ultrawide monitor. Instead of a curved panel like on other popular massive displays, it’s completely flat and gives you the screen real estate of two 27-inch, 1440p monitors running across your desk.

When connected to your PC or Mac, you can have two full-sized browser windows or apps running side by side. This makes the E49M1R an excellent choice for productivity, though with a 165Hz panel, Mini-LED backlighting, and AMD FreeSync Premium, it also provides a very immersive gaming experience — granted you have a PC powerful enough to run games at this monitor’s native resolution.

I’ve been using the E49M1R as my daily driver for a month now, and it’s definitely changed how I work. While I’ve used a standard 21:9 ultrawide display for almost a decade, jumping to 32:9 and all that extra screen space has made a real difference while multitasking. Still, it has its trade-offs. While this monitor offers dual HDMI and DisplayPort connections, it’s missing a USB-C port for a one-cable connection to your laptop. Likewise, due to its VA panel and sheer width, colors can appear washed out at the edges if you’re sitting too close.

My Innocn E49M1R review will help you decide if this is the best monitor for your workflow and your desk, or if it’s worth going with something smaller or slightly curved instead.

2 x HDMI 2.1, 2 x DisplayPort 1.4, 1 x audio out, 2 x USB-A, 1 x USB-B

47.82 × 1.99 × 14.43 inches (without stand), 47.82 × 9.31 × 21.44 inches (with stand)

The Innocn E49M1R is truly one of a kind, as there’s no other flat super ultrawide display this large. It takes up the full width of most desks, but in return, you get an impressively bright picture, plenty of screen real estate, enough input ports to connect four devices at once, and built-in speakers for the complete package.

At 47.82 x 1.99 x 14.43 inches, the E49M1R is the largest monitor I’ve ever unboxed. Just like with a large TV, I’d recommend having someone help you unpack it and install the included metal stand. In addition, you also get a power cord, an HDMI 2.1 cable, and a DisplayPort cable in the box. Unfortunately, there isn’t a USB-B cable included, which you’ll need if you want to take advantage of the E49M1R’s built-in USB hub — more on that later.

Just like with the other Innocn monitors I’ve tested, installing the metal stand is a breeze. It simply snaps into the back of the monitor, and a single thumb screw attaches the arm to its sturdy metal base. If you’d rather use one of the best monitor arms instead of the included stand, there are 100 x 100 VESA mounting holes on the back of the display.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

One thing I really appreciate about the E49M1R is that instead of tucking all the ports on the underside like you often see on other monitors, they’re all positioned on the back. Along with being height-adjustable, the stand features a cutout near the bottom to make routing cables up to the display easier.

Port-wise, you get dual HDMI 2.1 inputs and dual DisplayPort 1.4 connections, alongside an audio jack. There’s also a USB-B upstream port that, when connected to your computer, lets you use the two USB-A ports next to it for wireless dongles or a webcam. This isn’t a KVM (keyboard, video, mouse) switch, though, as you can’t share those peripherals across two separate computers. At the same time, there’s no USB-C port with Power Delivery, which feels like an odd omission on a premium, super ultrawide monitor like the E49M1R.

With the E49M1R unboxed and the stand installed, it was time to get it set up on my desk. Now a word of warning here — if you have a desk that’s 48 inches wide, you likely won’t have room for a full desktop PC, though you could tuck one of the best mini PCs underneath this massive display.

I set the E49M1R up on a desk shelf attached to the back of the Secretlab Magnus Evo, and even though that desk is 60 inches wide, things still felt a bit cramped. Fortunately, I’m in the process of reviewing the GMKtec Evo-X3, which is quite thin and designed to be used vertically.

So what’s it like sitting in front of a massive, 49-inch flat super ultrawide? It was definitely daunting at first, but after a few hours, my eyes and neck adjusted to the larger display. By default, you can position one app or browser window on either side, and this felt a lot like the dual-monitor setup I put together last year — just without a gap between the two screens.

While using the E49M1R with two Chrome windows side by side worked well enough, it wasn’t until I installed Microsoft’s PowerToys utility that I could take full advantage of this monitor. Using PowerToys’ built-in FancyZones window manager, I was able to split this 49-inch display into thirds, keeping a smaller window for video calls in the middle with two larger browser windows on either side for multitasking. This worked great, as I could look straight at the center of the screen while presenting and glance off to the side when I needed to check notes or respond to a quick message.

As someone who’s been using an ultrawide monitor for years, making the jump from 21:9 to 32:9 felt natural. If you’ve been using a standard 16:9 display on its own, though, you might be better off switching to a 21:9 ultrawide first before going all the way up to a super ultrawide — especially with a completely flat one like the E49M1R.

One thing you’ll likely have to deal with when switching to an ultrawide — or even a super ultrawide — monitor is black bars on the sides of most video content. However, when you find a video with the right aspect ratio for your screen, it’s a sight to behold.

To put the E49M1R’s video capabilities to the test, I scoured YouTube for 32:9 trailers until I found one for Godzilla vs. Kong. Seeing King Kong leaping across the landscape and fighting in Hollow Earth was downright awesome, and even though this was a compressed YouTube stream, the picture still looked fantastic on the E49M1R.

Based on our lab tests, you can see that while the E49M1R isn’t as bright as some other premium monitors when displaying content in SDR, it absolutely shines with HDR enabled — hitting a blistering 1,474 nits. It did fairly well with color accuracy, though this is a productivity monitor, and I wouldn’t recommend it for color grading or other heavy graphical work.

While 32:9 videos may be hard to find online, the same can’t be said for games. With a powerful gaming PC, you can fully immerse yourself in the action across the E49M1R’s entire 49-inch display.

Even though it was a tight fit, I managed to get the GMKtec Neo-X1 Pro set up on the side of the E49M1R and play some Red Dead Redemption 2. Riding on my horse across the Wild West as Arthur Morgan felt almost like a dream come true, as I could take in all the scenery thanks to the E49M1R’s wider field of view. I’m sure playing a racing game like Forza Horizon 6 would have been even better, though.

It’s worth noting that while the E49M1R has a 165Hz refresh rate with support for AMD FreeSync Premium, the display definitely lags behind the best gaming monitors when it comes to response time. At 8ms, it’s better suited for slower-paced games, which is why I tested it out with Red Dead Redemption 2 as opposed to a fast-paced, competitive shooter.

All in all, though, you can certainly play games on the E49M1R — even if it’s ultimately better suited for multi-window productivity tasks.

There’s truly no super ultrawide monitor quite like the Innocn E49M1R, thanks to its massive, completely flat display. However, that sheer width can cause colors on either side to look washed out depending on how close you’re sitting, and a USB-C port would have been a welcome addition.

Although this is the first super ultrawide monitor I’ve tested, I’ve actually spent quite a bit of time using two of Innocn’s ultrawide displays: the 40C1U and the 40C1R. While the former is a premium display with a 5K2K resolution and the latter is a more budget-friendly gaming monitor, both feature USB-C with Power Delivery.

Unfortunately, the E49M1R doesn’t. Now, I know some budget laptops would struggle to drive a massive display like this one, but most modern machines can handle it just fine. With Power Delivery built in, you also wouldn’t need to reach for your laptop charger — instead, you could just plug in your Windows laptop or MacBook and get right to work on the E49M1R’s 49-inch screen.

For a monitor with a list price of $999, the lack of a USB-C port is really puzzling, especially since I’ve tested much cheaper displays from Innocn that have one.

Now, whether you prefer a flat or curved ultrawide is something you’ll have to figure out on your own. Personally, I like flat ultrawides since they take up less space on my desk and can easily be wall-mounted or attached to a monitor arm.

With the E49M1R and its VA panel, however, its massive width creates a sort of optical illusion. Even though the picture on either side is just as bright as it is at the center, it doesn’t always appear that way — particularly when you’re sitting very close to the display. For instance, with three Chrome windows side by side, content on the outer two would appear washed out when I turned my head to look at it. However, if I pulled my office chair back a bit, it looked completely normal.

Now, if you’re dead set on having the largest, flattest super ultrawide monitor out there, I’d recommend pairing the E49M1R with a very deep desk. That way, you can position the monitor at the very back edge to mitigate this optical illusion. If you’re short on space, though, and aren’t using one of the best standing desks, you could always wall-mount this display just like you would a TV.

The Innocn E49M1R is truly one of a kind, and it’s a great fit for those who want as much screen real estate as possible without a multi-monitor setup or having to give up desk space for a curved display. That alone would be enough, but its Mini-LED backlighting really makes colors pop and blacks appear deeper, too. You also get plenty of ports alongside a built-in USB hub.

While I would have liked a built-in KVM switch as well, that isn’t necessarily a dealbreaker. Missing a USB-C port with Power Delivery could be a problem if you’re mainly a laptop user — though if you primarily use a desktop computer, this won’t be an issue, even if it still would have been a nice addition.

The Innocn E49M1R delivers and then some for anyone who wants the widest, flattest super ultrawide monitor you can get. At full price, you’re getting plenty of screen space for your buck — just make sure this display isn’t too wide for your setup and that you have a desk big enough to house it first.

#3053. Group 1 Automotive: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Unified branding and discounted oil-change campaigns are lifting repair traffic, helping offset pressure from vehicle affordability headwinds.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 28, 2026, Group 1 Automotive (GPI +1.14%) announced the acquisition of Hennessey Automotive Companies alongside a sweeping asset disposition plan. By swapping lower-margin dealerships for high-volume luxury locations, the auto retailer aims to expand margins and improve earnings durability. Controlling operating costs while capturing high-margin parts and service revenue remains key to surviving auto cycle volatility.

Group 1 is selling underperforming rooftops to acquire premium luxury locations that boost overall operating efficiency. The strategy lowers selling, general, and administrative (SG&A) expenses--the overhead required to run stores--while increasing adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA), a measure of core operating profitability.

Vehicle owners facing economic pressure frequently defect to independent repair shops as factory warranties expire. To protect parts and service traffic, Group 1 offers discounted door-buster promotions that bring drivers into service bays and yield larger overall repair orders.

Consolidating local store names under one national brand streamlines marketing expense and improves local store discovery. A single unified brand aggregates customer review scores across locations, helping stores rank higher in artificial intelligence search engines.

Customer pay service orders are rising as expanded bay capacity captures ongoing maintenance demand. Group 1 relies on overhead leverage and premium brand alignment to navigate tight vehicle affordability.

Debt reduction takes precedence over share repurchases as management works to lower leverage ratios following recent portfolio acquisitions.

#3050. Tired of paying for cloud storage every month? pCloud’s Black Friday Lifetime deal is the cure for subscription fatigue

Software used to be a one-time purchase, but over time, with the addition of cloud storage and services, everything has become a subscription. One company even tried to make your car seat heaters a subscription. Count the subscriptions you’re paying for right now: iCloud, a password manager, a couple of streaming services, a music service, maybe a VPN, and whatever other app decided this year that it needed to be $4.99 per month for something that used to be a one-time purchase.

Everything is a service now, and a lot of people are hitting the point where one more monthly charge is one too many on principle alone. Cloud storage is the one that’s hardest to cancel, because your photos and files are in it. That’s exactly why pCloud’s Lifetime plans are worth a look this Black Friday: you pay once, and your storage is yours for life!

Apple gives you 5 GB of iCloud for free, which stops being enough about a week after you buy an iPhone. The irony is that they launched with 5 GB of free storage in 2011, and it’s almost laughable that it hasn’t been increased since.

After that, it’s a subscription forever. The 2 TB iCloud+ plan costs $9.99 a month, about $120 a year, for as long as you want your photos to stay where they are. pCloud’s math is different. The 2 TB Lifetime plan is a one-time payment that costs less than four years of iCloud+ at the same size, and the day you buy it is the last day you pay anything for it.

If you’ve been paying for iCloud or Google Drive storage for all of your files for the last 9 years instead of using pCloud, go do the math on how much you’ve spent.

Apple charges a lot to move from a 256 GB MacBook Air to a 512 GB one, and you can’t change your mind later with a hard drive upgrade. Storage has gotten incredibly pricey in recent years as well. pCloud Drive is your solution without breaking the bank. It’s a native Mac app that mounts your pCloud storage as a drive in Finder, so your files appear as if they’re natively on your Mac but live in the cloud until you open them. A 256 GB laptop with a 2 TB pCloud Drive behind it stops feeling small. It runs on macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS, and Android, and everything stays in sync across all of them in real time.

With pCloud Backup, backing up the folders you choose is easy and safe from a lost laptop, fire, flood, or theft. If you run a NAS at home, pCloud supports backing it up via WebDAV, Rsync, SFTP, and SCP, making it a real offsite destination for a Synology NAS, not just a simple sync folder. It would be a perfect offsite backup for small businesses, remote workers, etc.

iCloud Photos is great, but it uses storage from your iCloud storage quota, which can get expensive as Apple’s cameras get better and better and file sizes keep increasing. Every pCloud plan includes pCloud Photos, a photo gallery that organizes everything by date on a timeline, automatically tags objects and scenes, and groups shots into albums by event and person.

The pCloud mobile app backs up your camera roll automatically to free up space on your iPhone; a Memories feature resurfaces older photos, as the Photos app does; and a built-in document scanner turns receipts and paperwork into PDFs without needing a separate app. Inside the app, there is also a built-in Photo Editor with crop, rotate, brightness, contrast, highlights, shadows, and eight one-click filters, so quick fixes don’t require moving it back to Apple Photos.

pCloud Docs covers documents, spreadsheets, presentations, PDFs, text, and markdown with six built-in editors and real-time collaboration, all from the browser or the mobile app. If your household is split, with one person on Microsoft, Apple, or Google, pCloud can pull in files from Google Photos, Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive, and Facebook. That’s the easiest way I’ve seen to get everyone’s files into one place without needing to download and reupload everything.

Files and photos aren’t the only benefit of joining the pCloud ecosystem. pCloud Pass is a password manager that works across all devices, browsers, and operating systems, with one-click login, form filling, and a generator for strong, unique passwords. Passwords are still hard, and most people are either paying monthly for a manager or reusing the same three passwords. A lifetime license solves the annoying aspects of using a dedicated password manager app or being locked into Apple’s or Google’s systems.

pCloud Encryption is client-side, zero-knowledge encryption for your most sensitive files. In plain language: files in your Crypto folder are encrypted on your Mac before they upload, and only you hold the key. pCloud can’t read them, and neither can anyone else. It’s the right place for tax returns, scans of your birth certificate, and anything else you’d rather not have sitting in a regular sync folder.

Here’s the deal you’ll want to pay the most attention to: pCloud offers an exclusive 3in1 Bundle, because it knocks out two more subscriptions at once. It’s 3 TB of Lifetime storage plus Lifetime pCloud Pass and Lifetime pCloud Encryption, and it’s the only offer that includes everything you need to ditch a vast majority of your subscriptions. Count up what this level of storage and functionality would cost you over three or four years, and you’ll see how incredible of a deal it is. If you don’t sign up today, you’ll end up regretting it in 2030.

pCloud’s Black Friday pricing runs from November 13 through November 28. Every plan is a one-time payment with Lifetime access, no subscription, and no renewal.

You also get to choose where your data is stored, with data centers in Luxembourg and the United States, and everything is protected in transit with TLS/SSL. With pCloud, it’s your files and your rules, and one Lifetime deal protects everything.

If you’re tired of paying for storage every month, this is the week to stop. Grab pCloud’s Black Friday Lifetime deal before it ends on November 28.

The best time to sign up for pCloud’s lifetime deal was 9 years ago. The second best is today.

#3048. Planet Labs PBC vs. Red Cat: Which Industrials Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Satellite scale meets drone agility, but one company's revenue jumped 508% while the other's forward multiple tells a very different valuation story.

Space and defense innovation are driving investor interest as hardware costs fall and demand for data rises. Choosing between Planet Labs PBC (PL -0.65%) and Red Cat (RCAT -3.43%) requires weighing satellite scale against drone agility.

Planet Labs focuses on geospatial data, capturing daily imagery used by government and commercial clients to monitor global changes. Red Cat provides robotic solutions, specifically unmanned aircraft for defense missions. While both companies target the defense and intelligence sectors, their underlying technologies and stages of financial development differ significantly.

Planet Labs provides geospatial data and Earth-imaging services, positioning it as a unique player among defense stocks and environmental monitoring firms. It serves over 700 customers, including various intelligence and defense agencies, by imaging Earth's landmass every day. Recent market analysis highlights its growing focus on sovereign satellite demand and on integrating imagery with Alphabet. A limited number of customers account for a substantial share of revenue, adding risk to the business.

In the 12 months ended July 31, 2026, revenue reached nearly $378.3 million, representing growth of approximately 44.1% compared to the prior period. Despite this top-line expansion, the company reported a net loss of nearly $359.9 million. This result reflects the high costs associated with maintaining its extensive satellite constellation and investing in its proprietary data analytics platforms.

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the current ratio is approximately 1.7x, indicating how well the company can cover short-term liabilities with its current assets. The debt-to-equity ratio is nearly 2.5x, meaning total debt, including short- and long-term obligations, is two and a half times shareholder equity. In the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, free cash flow was nearly $57.6 million. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 40.9% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation because it is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Red Cat focuses on providing advanced robotic solutions for the military and national security markets. In its latest annual report, the company disclosed that approximately 73% of its total revenue was generated from contracts with the U.S. Government. This high level of customer concentration risk is mitigated by strategic partnerships with AeroVironment (AVAV -2.75%) and Palantir Technologies (PLTR -2.09%) to enhance mission capabilities.

In the 12 months ended June 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $46.9 million, representing significant growth of approximately 508.2% over the prior year. Despite this rapid scaling, the company reported a net loss of nearly $101.0 million. This loss is primarily driven by heavy research and development spending as the company attempts to capture a larger share of the tactical drone market.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio is approximately 15.3x, indicating a strong ability to meet short-term obligations. The debt-to-equity ratio is nearly 0.1x, indicating the company carries very little debt relative to its shareholders' equity. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was nearly negative $95.8 million, reflecting the investment needed to scale its manufacturing and software capabilities.

Planet Labs PBC faces significant customer concentration, as a limited number of clients account for a substantial portion of its revenue. Operational risks include potential launch failures or hardware degradation within its satellite constellation. The company also faces competition from BlackSky Technology (BKSY +2.41%), Satellogic (SATL -6.25%), and Airbus (EADSF -0.98%), as well as from governments that provide free imagery.

Red Cat relies heavily on U.S. Government contracts, making it vulnerable to budget uncertainty and potential spending cuts. The company's active acquisition strategy carries integration risks, while competition from larger defense contractors remains intense. Additionally, it faces supply chain vulnerabilities, particularly regarding its reliance on third-party manufacturers for critical circuit chip sets.

Red Cat looks more attractive based on future earnings estimates, while Planet Labs trades at a slightly lower valuation relative to its sales over the past 12 months.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

When comparing Planet Labs and Red Cat, investors should consider a few key factors. Let's have a look at them and see what that tells us about each stock.

Firstly, we should consider revenue growth. On the surface, Red Cat wins the category, with average revenue growth of 995% compared to Planet Labs' 47%. However, with both companies, the revenue base is relatively small: $378 million for Planet Labs and $72 million for Red Cat. So while Red Cat is growing faster, this category is difficult to judge.

Another factor to consider is each company's balance sheet. Since neither company is profitable, it makes sense to examine their respective balance sheets. Planet Labs has no net debt, with over $368 million in cash on hand. Red Cat has no net debt, with over $310 million in cash on hand. That's important, as each company is still burning cash. Planet Labs has free cash flow of -$18 million over the last 12 months, while Red Cat has burned through about $157 million. Since it has a longer cash runway, Planet Labs gains an edge in this category.

Finally, there's valuation. We'll examine price-to-sales (P/S) multiples, since neither company is profitable. Red Cat is more affordable, with a P/S ratio of 6.3x, while Planet Labs' 12.2x multiple is higher.

To sum up, investors may want to take a closer look at each of these growth stocks. However, in the direct head-to-head matchup, I view Planet Labs as the winner, given its longer cash runway, which is vitally important to stocks at this early stage.

Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

I’ve spent the past few weeks thinking about how Apple built up the best deal in enterprise AI. Two things happened that make me think Apple knew that all along (or maybe they didn’t and got lucky). Meta released its most capable open-weight model yet and optimized it to run on a Mac Studio. I also spent time with Osaurus, an app that runs a usable local AI model on something as small as a 16 GB Apple silicon laptop without needing a network connection. They even have two models that will run on 8 GB.

The Xserve has been dead since 2011, but its spiritual successor sits on a desk rather than in a rack.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

For the last few years, the narrative has been that Apple fell behind in AI because it didn’t have a frontier model. Siri AI got delayed, and the Apple Intelligence rollout was not great. In hindsight, I think Apple was right not to run that race, as the frontier-model business has turned into somewhat of a capital bonfire. Every frontier lab is spending billions on GPUs to be the best for a few months at a time, and the moment a model is good enough, someone else releases an open-weight version that runs on hardware you already own.

Open-weight models prove it: Muse Spark Open has 816 billion parameters, 42 billion active parameters, and a million-token context window, and Meta is giving it away. Apple didn’t build that LLM. It built the hardware that runs it. With that being said, Siri is still far behind.

Look at what Apple has shipped while everyone was waiting on them to try to compete with Anthropic or OpenAI. With Apple silicon’s unified memory, the GPU can use up to 512 GB of memory on a single Mac Studio, instead of being limited to whatever fits on a graphics card.

MLX is Apple’s machine learning framework, and it’s built specifically for the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon. If you’ve used NumPy, the API will feel familiar right away. On top of that, MLX includes higher-level packages for neural networks and optimizers, along with function transformations for automatic differentiation and graph optimization, so you can build more complex models without giving up efficiency. It also has bindings in Swift, C++, and C, which means it runs on any Apple platform.

Apple’s own Machine Learning Research post shows four M5 Ultra Mac Studios running Muse Spark Open at over 36 tokens per second, which is faster than you can read, while peaking around 300 watts per machine.

Apple’s unified memory architecture lets the M5 Ultra’s integrated GPU use up to 512 GB per Mac Studio, so two machines can hold an entire model. And the chip’s 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth is fast enough to read the small slice each token needs. The result is two Mac Studios behave like one supercomputer with a terabyte of unified memory.

We tested a range of agentic workflows running entirely on-device, using Muse Code powered by Muse Spark Open, including shipping real iOS changes to Ice Cubes (an open-source Mastodon client) — bug fixes, new features, full build — and driving DaVinci Resolve end to end, with the model reviewing footage frame by frame to find the strongest moments and crop them vertically.

That’s the Xserve pitch, rebuilt for 2026. Apple killed the Xserve in 2011 because nobody wanted a Mac in a data center. The Mac mini came along and provided some new use cases over the years. Now, a couple of Mac Studios can host a model that would otherwise require a rack of Nvidia hardware and a power budget to match, and it does so quietly enough to sit under a desk. Apple wasn’t trying to compete with OpenAI, Anthropic, or Nvidia. It was building the infrastructure for everything except the frontier model, and it looks like that’s where the market is going. A company like MacStadium has to be loving this future as well.

The Mac Studio story is the headline, but what matters most to most IT teams is at the other end of the lineup. I had Terence Pae, co-founder and CEO of Osaurus, on the Apple @ Work podcast last week. Osaurus is a free, open-source AI tool for the Mac. It helps manage local models that work offline, but it can also call a frontier model when needed. A really cool feature, when it does this, is that Osaurus runs a small local model first to find names, phone numbers, and account numbers in whatever you pasted, and swaps them for placeholders before anything goes to Claude or OpenAI.

Osaurus has no servers and no customer database. If the company went out of business tomorrow, the app would keep running until macOS broke it. Individuals use it for free. Workspaces, the paid tier, is for teams who want to share agents across their own Macs. There’s a Windows beta as well, which I think helps Apple’s case more than it hurts it. When the same app runs on both platforms, the Mac’s unified memory is the difference.

In talking with him, Terence mentioned he wouldn’t be surprised if a local model matches what today’s frontier models can do by this time next year. I believe him, and that’s the point. The frontier will keep moving, but good enough keeps moving too, and good enough is what most employees need most of the day. Apple spent the AI race building memory, bandwidth, and a framework instead of trying to match the frontier, and the narrative was that they were behind.

Now the most capable open-weight model in the US is optimized for the Mac.

#3046. Here’s a HomeView feature that should come to every Apple device

This week, Apple started shipping the HomeView, its first display made for the smart home. On the HomeView, there’s one particularly nice feature that I’d love to see make its way to all Apple platforms: Ambient Dark Mode.

On iOS, iPadOS, and macOS today – the only flexibility you have on dark mode is whether or not it automatically switches on towards night time. While this is generally helpful and certainly appreciated, it isn’t super granular. Of course, you can adjust the time when it switches, but generally speaking its just a one time toggle.

With HomeView, you can enable ambient dark mode. In display settings, once you enable automatic dark mode, there’s the usual two settings you’d see on other Apple platforms: sunrise to sunset, as well as a custom schedule. HomeView takes it a step further with ambient mode, where the ambient light sensor determines whether or not you should be in light or dark mode.

Of course, a sunrise to sunset schedule generally works for most cases. However, if you’re up late at night with your lights turned on, you still might prefer light mode in an instance where macOS would generally be in dark mode. Similarly, if you wake up later in the day with your curtains shut, at say 11am, you might not want to immediately see light mode on your phone the second you open your eyes.

There are tons of good reasons for why someone would prefer ambient light-based automatic light and dark mode switching. HomeView software is the first Apple platform to enable this, and I’d love to see it come to iPhone, iPad, and Mac starting next year with OS 28.

#3045. Indie App Spotlight: ‘Milton’ lets you turn your old iPad into a home dashboard

Welcome to Indie App Spotlight. This is a weekly 9to5Mac series where we showcase the latest apps in the indie app world. If you’re a developer and would like your app featured, get in contact.

Apple finally released its new HomeView this week, a smart display that serves at the center of your home. What if you don’t want to buy a new product though? Milton is an app for older iPads running iPadOS 17 and later that can serve a similar purpose.

Milton offers a customizable dashboard that allows you to put your most important tiles front and center. It can show your calendar, chores, shopping lists, weather, the clock, a photo frame, a to do list, and so much more. Everything you include will show on the family iPad, but it can also sync to iPhones if you want to check something remotely.

There’s one neat feature that’ll be fun for families: a points system. If your kids complete chores, they can be awarded points and as a parent you can set goals for what kids can earn with enough points. This system can be used to encourage kids to complete chores or follow routines. Parents can also sign off on the chores to ensure kids aren’t just tapping the complete button.

It also serves as a nice recipe guide. If you take photos of cookbooks, Milton can parse through what you captured and provide a step by step guide for cooking. If you don’t have certain ingredients, it can quickly be added to your shoping list.

This only scratches the surface of what Milton can do. You can read their website for the rest.

Here’s why Josh, the developer, decided to build Milton:

I’m a software engineer, and my partner is an oncology pharmacist. She wanted one place that kept our household organised: the calendar, the chores, the shopping, what’s for dinner. Skylight is expensive, and the iPad apps that do this charge a subscription every year. We wanted something that fit our lives, connected us as the Apple family we already are, and didn’t cost families a fortune.

Like most families, we had an old iPad lying around. We put it in a case with a magnet, stuck it to the fridge, and that became Milton.

Milton provides a very generous free offering on the App Store. The core organizer features are all available out of the box, but if you want to add more people to the app, sync across devices, or share the app with other family members (for their personal devices), you’ll need to purchase Milton Individual for $4.99 (one time purchase) or Milton Family for $14.99. Milton Family automatically shares with your iCloud family sharing group.
